title: Level 2 · Conditional Statements and Loops
blurb: Make decisions with if statements and repeat work with for and while loops.

lessons.title: If Statement
lessons.concept: An if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is True. Write if condition: and indent the lines that belong to it. If the condition is False, Python simply skips the indented block.
lessons.why: Programs constantly make choices: show a discount only if the bill is large, or let a user in only if the password matches.
lessons.example:
marks = 72
if marks >= 40:
    print('You passed!')
print('Done')
lessons.example_note: Prints 'You passed!' because the condition is true, then always prints 'Done'.
lessons.prompt: Read a mark as an integer. If it is 40 or more, print You passed!. After the if block, always print Result checked.
lessons.starter:
marks = int(input())
# if marks >= 40, print 'You passed!'
# then print 'Result checked' (outside the if)
lessons.solution:
marks = int(input())
if marks >= 40:
    print('You passed!')
print('Result checked')
hints: Start with: if marks >= 40:
The line under the if must be indented with 4 spaces.
Put print('Result checked') back at the left edge, so it always runs.

lessons.title: If Else
lessons.concept: else gives the other path: it runs when the if condition is False. Exactly one of the two blocks runs. Write else: at the same indentation as if.
lessons.why: Yes/no decisions are everywhere: can the user vote, is the item in stock, is the payment successful.
lessons.example_note: Prints 'Minor' because 15 is not 18 or more.
lessons.prompt: Read an age as an integer. If the age is 18 or more print Eligible to vote, otherwise print Not eligible.
hints: You need both an if and an else.
else: has no condition after it.
if age >= 18: print('Eligible to vote') / else: print('Not eligible')

lessons.title: If Elif Else
lessons.concept: When there are more than two choices, use elif (short for 'else if'). Python checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs the first one that is true; else catches everything left.
lessons.why: Grades, tax slabs, delivery charges and shipping zones all have several ranges.
lessons.example_note: 82 is not 90 or more, but is 75 or more, so it prints B.
lessons.prompt: Read marks as an integer and print a grade: A for 90 or more, B for 75 or more, C for 50 or more, otherwise Fail.
lessons.starter:
marks = int(input())
# use if / elif / else
hints: Check the highest range first.
Use elif for the middle ranges.
if >= 90 -> A, elif >= 75 -> B, elif >= 50 -> C, else -> Fail.

lessons.title: Nested If
lessons.concept: You can put an if inside another if. The inner check only happens when the outer condition is true. Indent the inner block one more level.
lessons.why: Real checks come in steps: first is the amount valid, and only then is there enough balance.
lessons.example_note: Checks login first, then the role; prints 'User page'.
lessons.prompt: Read a balance and then a withdrawal amount (both integers). If the amount is more than 0, then: print Withdrawal successful if it is not more than the balance, otherwise Insufficient balance. If the amount is 0 or less, print Invalid amount.
lessons.starter:
balance = int(input())
amount = int(input())
# outer if: amount > 0
#     inner if/else: compare with balance
# else: Invalid amount
hints: First check the amount is valid with an outer if.
Inside it, write a second if/else comparing amount with balance.
The final else (Invalid amount) lines up with the outer if.

lessons.title: Ternary Operator
lessons.concept: The ternary operator is a one-line if/else that gives a value: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false. It is handy for picking one of two values to store or print.
lessons.why: Short choices such as a 'Free' or 'Paid' label, or 'Open' or 'Closed', fit neatly in one line.
lessons.example:
age = 20
status = 'Adult' if age >= 18 else 'Minor'
print(status)
lessons.example_note: Stores 'Adult' in status in a single line.
lessons.prompt: Read an integer n. Using a one-line ternary expression stored in result, set it to Even or Odd, then print result.
lessons.starter:
n = int(input())
# result = ... if ... else ...
# print(result)
lessons.solution:
n = int(input())
result = 'Even' if n % 2 == 0 else 'Odd'
print(result)
hints: The pattern is: A if condition else B.
n % 2 == 0 is true for even numbers.
result = 'Even' if n % 2 == 0 else 'Odd'

lessons.title: For Loop
lessons.concept: A for loop repeats a block once for every item in a sequence. In for letter in word:, the variable letter takes each character in turn. Indent the lines you want repeated.
lessons.why: Going through every product in a cart, every student in a class or every line of a file is a for loop.
lessons.example_note: Prints each fruit on its own line.
lessons.prompt: Read a word. Use a for loop to print each letter of the word on its own line.
lessons.starter:
word = input()
# for letter in word: print it
hints: A string is a sequence of letters, so you can loop over it.
for letter in word:
Indent print(letter) under the for line.

lessons.title: While Loop
lessons.concept: A while loop repeats as long as its condition stays True. Something inside the loop must change the condition (like n -= 1), otherwise it runs forever.
lessons.why: Use it when you do not know in advance how many repeats you need: keep asking until the input is valid, or count down a timer.
lessons.example:
n = 3
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1
print('Go!')
lessons.prompt: Read an integer n. Use a while loop to count down from n to 1, one number per line, then print Liftoff!.
lessons.starter:
n = int(input())
# while n > 0: print n, then reduce it
# finally print 'Liftoff!'
lessons.solution:
n = int(input())
while n > 0:
    print(n)
    n -= 1
print('Liftoff!')
hints: The loop should run while n is greater than 0.
Do not forget n -= 1 inside the loop.
Print 'Liftoff!' after the loop, at the left edge.

lessons.title: Nested Loops
lessons.concept: A loop inside a loop is a nested loop: the inner loop runs completely for every step of the outer loop. range(3) gives 0, 1, 2 (you will learn it fully in a later lesson). Use print('*', end='') to stay on the same line.
lessons.why: Tables, grids, seating plans and patterns are built with loops inside loops.
lessons.prompt: Read an integer n. Print a triangle: row 1 has 1 star, row 2 has 2 stars, up to row n with n stars. Use range(1, n + 1) for the rows and a nested loop for the stars.
lessons.starter:
n = int(input())
for row in range(1, n + 1):
    # inner loop: print row stars on one line
    pass
hints: The inner loop should repeat 'row' times.
print('*', end='') keeps stars on one line; a plain print() ends the row.
for star in range(row): print('*', end='') then print() after it.

lessons.title: Break
lessons.concept: break stops a loop immediately, even if the loop condition is still true. Combined with while True: it gives a loop that runs until something special happens.
lessons.why: Programs keep reading input until the user types 'quit', or stop searching once an item is found.
lessons.prompt: Read numbers one per line and add them to a total. When the number 0 is read, stop the loop with break and print the total.
lessons.starter:
total = 0
while True:
    n = int(input())
    # if n is 0: break
    # otherwise add it to total
# print total
lessons.solution:
total = 0
while True:
    n = int(input())
    if n == 0:
        break
    total += n
print(total)
hints: Check for 0 right after reading the number.
if n == 0: break
Add with total += n after the if, and print total after the loop.

lessons.title: Continue
lessons.concept: continue skips the rest of the current round and jumps to the next one. The loop itself keeps going; only this round is cut short.
lessons.why: Skipping bad data, such as blank rows or invalid entries, while still processing everything else.
lessons.example_note: Prints 1 2 4 5 (each on its own line), skipping 3.
lessons.prompt: Read 5 daily sales amounts (one per line). A negative amount is a wrong entry: skip it with continue. Print the total of the valid amounts.
lessons.starter:
total = 0
for day in range(5):
    amount = int(input())
    # if amount is negative: continue
    # add amount to total
# print total
lessons.solution:
total = 0
for day in range(5):
    amount = int(input())
    if amount < 0:
        continue
    total += amount
print(total)
hints: Test amount < 0 before adding.
if amount < 0: continue
total += amount comes after the if; print(total) after the loop.

lessons.title: Pass
lessons.concept: pass is a statement that does nothing. Python needs at least one line inside every block, so pass is a placeholder when you have not written the code yet.
lessons.why: Developers sketch the structure of a program first and use pass to fill in the blanks later.
lessons.example_note: Prints nothing, because the passing branch is an empty placeholder.
lessons.prompt: Read a mark as an integer. If it is 40 or more, leave the block as just pass (placeholder). Otherwise print Needs improvement. Finally print Checked.
lessons.starter:
mark = int(input())
# if mark >= 40: use pass
# else: print 'Needs improvement'
# always print 'Checked'
hints: An empty if block is an error, so write pass in it.
The else branch prints the message.
print('Checked') goes at the left edge at the end.

lessons.title: Range
lessons.concept: range(start, stop, step) makes a sequence of numbers. It stops before stop. range(5) is 0-4, range(1, 6) is 1-5 and range(2, 11, 2) is 2, 4, 6, 8, 10.
lessons.why: Whenever you need to repeat something a set number of times, or count by 2s, 5s or 10s, you use range.
lessons.prompt: Read an integer n. Use a for loop with range (with a step of 2) to print all even numbers from 2 up to n, one per line. Then print Done.
lessons.starter:
n = int(input())
# for i in range(2, ?, 2): print(i)
# then print 'Done'
lessons.solution:
n = int(input())
for i in range(2, n + 1, 2):
    print(i)
print('Done')
hints: Start at 2 and step by 2.
The stop value is excluded, so use n + 1.
for i in range(2, n + 1, 2):

lessons.title: Loop Else
lessons.concept: A loop can have an else block. It runs when the loop finishes without hitting break. If break happens, the else is skipped.
lessons.why: It is a neat way to do 'search the list; if not found, say so' without extra flag variables.
lessons.example_note: No even number is found, so the loop's else prints the message.
lessons.prompt: The roll numbers present today are [101, 102, 103, 104]. Read a roll number. Loop through the list: if it matches, print Present and break. Use a loop else to print Absent when no match was found.
lessons.starter:
present = [101, 102, 103, 104]
roll = int(input())
# for r in present: if r == roll -> print 'Present' and break
# else: print 'Absent'
hints: The else lines up with for, not with if.
break skips the loop's else.
for r in present: if r == roll: print('Present'); break  /  else: print('Absent')
